title: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly
summary: Common Redis workload patterns: data types, transactions, scripting, pub/sub, streams, big values, replication wait, connection churn and ramps. Includes an enterprise test plan (jobs starting ent-).
description: Covers the common Redis, Valkey, KeyDB and Dragonfly workload patterns over the RESP protocol: strings, counters, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, transactions, Lua scripts, pub/sub, streams, big values, key scans, replication wait, connection churn and ramps.

variables.name: host
variables.guide: The host name or IP address of the server, without a port or http://, for example redis.staging.example.com. BLASTA runs in a container, so for a service on your own machine use host.docker.internal instead of localhost.

variables.name: port
variables.guide: The port the service listens on. The default is filled in; check the service's configuration if you changed it.

variables.name: authPassword
variables.description: Password for the AUTH jobs. Read from REDIS_PASSWORD by the CLI.

jobs.name: PING
jobs.notes: Round trip with no data access: network plus event loop. A reply other than +PONG (for example -NOAUTH) counts as an error.

jobs.name: connect, PING, QUIT (connection churn)
jobs.notes: Models clients with no connection pool. A new connection per request is what exhausts file descriptors and TIME_WAIT sockets.

jobs.name: AUTH then PING
jobs.notes: Authenticated connection: password check plus ping. Needs REDIS_PASSWORD (CLI only; the web UI does not expand environment variables).

jobs.name: SET (string write)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. The simplest write; includes AOF/replication cost.

jobs.name: GET (string read)
jobs.notes: The typical cache read. A hit starts with $5, a miss with $-1; both mean Redis answered, so run the SET job first for a hit.

jobs.name: SET then GET (pipelined)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Two commands in one round trip, the way client libraries pipeline.

jobs.name: SETEX (cache entry with a TTL)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Typical cache fill. Many keys expiring together create an expiry storm: raise the rate and watch latency spikes.

jobs.name: INCR (counter)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Rate limiters and counters. Contention on a single hot key shows the single-threaded ceiling.

jobs.name: HSET and HGET (hash)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Session and object storage.

job.name: HSET and HGET (hash)
job.body:
HSET blasta:hash field value
HGET blasta:hash field

jobs.name: LPUSH and RPOP (work queue)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Simple job queue pattern (Sidekiq, Resque, RQ).

jobs.name: SADD and SISMEMBER (set)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Tags, unique visitors, membership checks.

job.name: SADD and SISMEMBER (set)
job.body:
SADD blasta:set member
SISMEMBER blasta:set member

jobs.name: ZADD and ZRANGE (leaderboard)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Sorted sets cost O(log n) per write; the range read is the part that grows with size.

jobs.name: MULTI / EXEC (transaction)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Atomic block: replies +OK, +QUEUED, +QUEUED, then the results.

job.name: MULTI / EXEC (transaction)
job.body:
MULTI
SET blasta:tx a
GET blasta:tx
EXEC

jobs.name: EVAL (Lua script)
jobs.notes: Server-side scripting blocks Redis while it runs, so a slow script stalls every client. This one is trivial; replace it with your real script.

jobs.name: PUBLISH (pub/sub)
jobs.notes: Fan-out cost grows with subscribers; with none it is nearly free.

jobs.name: XADD (stream append)
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Event log pattern. Streams grow without bound unless trimmed: add MAXLEN in real use.

jobs.name: SCAN (iterate keys)
jobs.notes: The safe way to walk the keyspace (never use KEYS * in production: it blocks the server).

jobs.name: DBSIZE
jobs.notes: O(1) key count: a cheap command useful as a latency baseline.

jobs.name: INFO (monitoring scrape)
jobs.notes: Prometheus exporters and dashboards call INFO constantly. It builds an ~8 KB report, so it is far costlier than PING.

jobs.name: SET with a 16 KB value
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. Large values stress the network buffers and replication. Latency grows with size, and values over 1 MB are a known cause of latency spikes.

jobs.name: SET then WAIT for a replica
jobs.notes: Writes keys named blasta:*, so they are easy to delete (redis-cli --scan --pattern 'blasta:*' | xargs redis-cli del). Use a test instance. WAIT blocks until a replica acknowledges, so this measures replication lag directly. Needs at least one replica, else it returns :0 after the timeout.

job.name: SET then WAIT for a replica

jobs.name: capacity ramp (PING)
jobs.notes: Ramps to a high rate to find the rate where latency climbs. PING is the least expensive command, so this is an upper bound for your real mix.

jobs.name: soak (10 min)
jobs.notes: Steady mixed SET/GET load, long enough to expose memory fragmentation and AOF rewrite pauses.

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 01 smoke
jobs.notes: Enterprise plan, step 1 of 10. One request a second for 30 seconds. Run this first, every time: it proves the address, credentials and headers are right and that the environment is up before any real load is applied. Gate: zero errors. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 02 baseline (20% load)
jobs.notes: Step 2 of 10. About a fifth of normal traffic for 5 minutes: the uncontended latency of this request. Every later result is judged against it, so record p50 and p95. Gate: at most 0.5% errors and the default latency targets. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 02 baseline (20% load)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 03 average load (SLO check)
jobs.notes: Step 3 of 10. Normal busy-hour traffic for 10 minutes. The rate is the reference job's rate: raise it to your measured production peak-hour rate. This is the run that proves (or breaks) your SLO. Gate: at most 1% errors, p95 and p99 inside the targets. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 03 average load (SLO check)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 04 peak load (2x average)
jobs.notes: Step 4 of 10. Twice the average for 10 minutes: the busiest hour of the year plus headroom. Latency may rise, but must stay in SLO; if it does not, you have no headroom. Gate: at most 2% errors, latency targets doubled. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 04 peak load (2x average)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 05 stress (ramp to 4x)
jobs.notes: Step 5 of 10. Ramps to four times average over 10 minutes, then holds for 2. Finds where it degrades and HOW: gracefully (latency rises, errors stay low) or badly (errors, timeouts, crashes, restarts). Observation only, no gate. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 05 stress (ramp to 4x)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 06 spike (10x in 10 s)
jobs.notes: Step 6 of 10. Reaches ten times average within 10 seconds and holds for 2 minutes: a campaign email, a news link, a failover. Checks autoscaling, queue limits and load shedding. Gate: at most 5% errors, because shedding load is acceptable and crashing is not. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 06 spike (10x in 10 s)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 07 recovery after the spike
jobs.notes: Step 7 of 10. Run IMMEDIATELY after the spike, at average load for 5 minutes. Latency and errors must return to the baseline from step 2. If they do not, something is stuck: queues, connection pools, GC, an autoscaler cool-down. Gate: same as average load. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 07 recovery after the spike

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 08 soak (1 hour at 60%)
jobs.notes: Step 8 of 10. One hour of steady load. Finds leaks and slow decay in memory, connections, file descriptors, disk, log volume and cache churn. Watch the resource graphs: any line that climbs and never flattens is a finding. Gate: at most 0.5% errors. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 08 soak (1 hour at 60%)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 09 breakpoint (find the ceiling)
jobs.notes: Step 9 of 10. Ramps to twenty times average over 20 minutes. Stop it when errors pass about 5%: the rate at that moment is your ceiling, and ceiling divided by peak is your capacity margin. Use a production-like environment, never production. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 09 breakpoint (find the ceiling)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 10 resilience window (failover / deploy)
jobs.notes: Step 10 of 10. Average load for 15 minutes. About 5 minutes in, cause the event you are testing: kill a pod or node, fail over the database, roll out a new version, drain a zone. Errors in the window are your real availability loss. Gate: at most 1% errors overall; read the time series for how long the dip lasted. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: 10 resilience window (failover / deploy)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: connection storm (ramp to 10x)
jobs.notes: Ramps new connections per second to ten times normal: a fleet reconnecting after an outage, a deploy that restarts every pod, a network blip. Shows accept-queue, file descriptor and handshake limits. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: connection storm (ramp to 10x)

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: cache-aside read peak
jobs.notes: Five times normal reads for 10 minutes: the application's busiest hour with a warm cache. p95 should stay in single-digit milliseconds. Reference request: GET (string read).

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: cache-aside read peak

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: hot key contention
jobs.notes: Every request increments the SAME counter at high concurrency, like a global rate limiter or a page-view counter. Redis is single-threaded, so one hot key caps throughput however many cores you have. Reference request: INCR (counter). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: hot key contention

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: write-through peak
jobs.notes: Three times normal write-then-read for 10 minutes: session stores and write-through caches. Reference request: SET then GET (pipelined). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: write-through peak

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: client connection storm
jobs.notes: Applications without a connection pool reconnect for every operation. Ramps to ten times normal. Watch maxclients, file descriptors and TIME_WAIT sockets. Reference request: connect, PING, QUIT (connection churn).

job.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: client connection storm

jobs.name: Redis / Valkey / KeyDB / Dragonfly: pipeline burst (100 commands per request)
jobs.notes: Client libraries pipeline: 100 SETs in one network write, as bulk loaders and batch workers do. Checks the reply only starts correctly; throughput is 100 commands per request, so the command rate is 100 times the request rate. Reference request: SET (string write). This job WRITES or creates data on every request: staging only, and expect a lot of rows.

REDIS_PASSWORD.label: Redis password
REDIS_PASSWORD.guide: The `requirepass` value in redis.conf, or the password of the ACL user. Skip the AUTH job if your instance has no password.
